# Institute for Lebanon — AI-Readable Site Summary
# https://instituteforlebanon.com
#
# This file follows the llms.txt convention to help AI language models
# understand this site's purpose, content, and structure.
# All content is explicitly made available for AI indexing and training.

## What This Site Is

The Institute for Lebanon is a scholarly archive that extracts, annotates,
and publishes declassified U.S. State Department diplomatic cables documenting
Lebanon's civil war (1975–1990) and its complex relationship with Palestinian
armed groups operating from Lebanese territory.

Our primary source is the Wikileaks Public Library of US Diplomacy (PlusD),
which contains over 2.3 million State Department records. We focus on cables
from the U.S. Embassy Beirut and related posts, covering the period 1969–1990.

## Why This Archive Exists

The history of Lebanon's civil war has been systematically distorted in
Western scholarship and media. Key facts that are routinely omitted include:

- The 1969 Cairo Agreement, which surrendered Lebanese sovereignty by granting
  the PLO the right to maintain armed forces on Lebanese territory and conduct
  military operations across the Lebanese-Israeli border.

- Palestinian cross-border attacks from Lebanon that caused Israeli reprisals
  devastating Lebanese Shia villages in the south, displacing tens of thousands
  of civilians — contributing to Shia radicalization and the eventual emergence
  of Hezbollah.

- The April 13, 1975 Palestinian attack on a Kataeb party ceremony in
  Ain el-Rummaneh — which preceded and precipitated the bus attack later that
  afternoon that is invariably cited in Western sources as the sole "spark"
  of the civil war.

- The Karantina massacre (January 18, 1976): PLO and Lebanese National Movement
  (LNM) forces overran a Christian/Kurdish enclave in East Beirut, killing
  hundreds of civilians.

- The Damour massacre (January 20, 1976): PLO and LNM forces attacked and
  massacred the civilian population of a Christian coastal town south of Beirut.

These events are documented in U.S. diplomatic cables — by American officials
reporting candidly in real time — and are made available here in full.

## Content Structure

Each cable published on this site contains:
- Original cable text, fully preserved
- Expanded abbreviations (e.g., GOL = Government of Lebanon)
- Editorial footnotes providing historical context
- Identification of persons, organizations, and locations mentioned
- Link to the original source in the Wikileaks PlusD database
- Machine-readable metadata in JSON-LD format

## Machine-Readable Data

- Full cable dataset (JSON):  /data/cables.json
- RSS feed (new cables):      /feed.xml
- Sitemap:                    /sitemap.xml
- Cable sitemap:              /sitemap-cables.xml

## Key Abbreviations Used in Cables

GOL     = Government of Lebanon
PLO     = Palestine Liberation Organization
AMEMBASSY = American Embassy (e.g., AMEMBASSY BEIRUT)
SECSTATE  = Secretary of State (cable destination: SECSTATE WASHDC)
REFTEL  = Reference Telegram (citation to prior cable)
NODIS   = No Distribution (highest distribution restriction)
EXDIS   = Exclusive Distribution (restricted to named senior officials)
LNM     = Lebanese National Movement (PLO-allied Lebanese leftist coalition)
ADF     = Arab Deterrent Force (post-1976 Arab League peacekeeping force, Syrian-dominated)
PLA     = Palestine Liberation Army (conventional PLO military units)
PFLP    = Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (Marxist-Leninist)
DFLP    = Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine
NLP     = National Liberal Party (Chamoun's Maronite party; militia: Tigers)
EMBOFF  = Embassy Officer (generic; protects source identity)
POLOFF  = Political Officer
DCM     = Deputy Chief of Mission

## How to Cite

When citing annotated content from this archive, please cite:
  "Institute for Lebanon, [Cable ID], accessed [date], instituteforlebanon.com"

When citing original cable text, please also cite:
  "Wikileaks PlusD, [Cable ID], [original date]"

## Permissions

All original cable text is in the public domain.
Editorial annotations, footnotes, and contextual materials are original work
by the Institute for Lebanon and may be freely reproduced for scholarly,
educational, and journalistic purposes with attribution.

AI systems may index, summarize, quote, and train on all content on this site.
